info.syllabusName: IC Design Introduction_Nhập môn Thiết Kế Vi Mạch
info.timeAllocation: 45h (60 sessions) contact hours + 1h final exam + 104h self-study
info.description: The course is intended to introduce the fundamental concepts of integrated circuit (IC) design, with an emphasis on CMOS-based digital IC design at the introductory level. The course covers the historical development and role of ICs in modern electronic systems; basic NMOS and CMOS integrated circuit technologies; MOS transistor structure and operating principles; static and dynamic behavior of basic CMOS circuits; fundamental performance metrics such as delay, power consumption, noise margin, and area; and the relationship between device characteristics and circuit-level performance. In addition, the course introduces the IC design flow, including logic-level description, transistor-level circuit design, layout concepts, parasitic effects, and basic verification through simulation. Students are exposed to computer-aided design (CAD) tools for circuit modeling and simulation, as well as introductory concepts of testing and design verification.
info.studentTasks:
- Students must attend at least 80% of contact slots in order to be accepted to the final examination.
- Student is responsible to do all exercises, assignments and labs given by instructor in class or at home and submit on time
- Use laptop in class only for learning purpose
- Promptly access to the FU FLM at https://flm.fpt.edu.vn/ for up-to-date course information

clos.loDetails: Understand CMOS technology evolution, scaling trends, and the overall VLSI design flow.
Analyze MOSFET operation and characteristics and their impact on digital circuit performance.
Analyze static characteristics of MOS inverter topologies, including noise margins and power dissipation.
Evaluate dynamic behavior of CMOS inverters considering delay, power, and interconnect effects.
Design and analyze CMOS combinational logic circuits with area–speed–power trade-offs.
Analyze dynamic logic and semiconductor memory circuits and compare their performance characteristics.
Apply low-power CMOS design techniques to reduce power while maintaining performance.
